Odd Scoring

Game StrategyParity

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: you and the computer take turns moving one chip to the left end. Then each counts the steps they made, and the one with an even number wins.
How to play: pick a cell 1, 2 or 3 steps to the left of the chip to move it there. You go first.

Slide the band sideways to see all of it.

Look for the math

Reaching the end first is not the point here: the last move wins nothing by itself. What counts is whether your own steps add up to an even number. The band always has an odd number of steps, so one total is even and the other odd, and there is never a draw.

Work back from the end

One step from the end you have no choice. If your total so far is even, that step makes it odd and you lose; if it is odd, you win. Two steps away you may take 1 or 2, so pick the one that makes your total even, and so on. This way of solving a game from its last move is called backward induction. Each position needs only two facts: how many steps are left, and the parity of your own total.

The pattern repeats every 8

Carry that on and the positions where the player about to move is lost are:

your total is even: 1, 4, 9, 12, 17, 20, 25 steps left
your total is odd: 5, 8, 13, 16, 21, 24 steps left

In other words, the steps left leave a remainder of 1 or 4 when divided by 8 if your total is even, and 0 or 5 if it is odd. A winning move is one that hands the computer such a position. You start with a total of 0, which is even, so you can win every band except those of 1, 9, 17 and 25 steps. From 11 steps the winning first move is 2.

What the computer knows

The original page says the computer plays the simpler game of Scoring until the chip is 9 cells from the left, and only then pays attention to parity. That is what the applet does, and this page keeps it. Far from the end the computer leaves you a multiple of 4 steps (the Modular hint marks those cells); with 7 or fewer left it plays the table above without a mistake. But the Scoring rule is not the right one for this game: we checked every position, and beyond 7 steps the computer misses a winning move in 13 of them. So you can be sure of beating it from 17 and 25 steps too, where a perfect opponent would beat you. From 9 steps you win only if its random move goes wrong, and from 1 step never.

The hints

Forward numbers each cell by the steps from the start, Backward counts the cells from the left, and Modular puts a dot on every fourth cell from the end. This page also shows the steps each player has made so far, which the applet left for you to keep in your head, and you press a cell where the applet had you drag the chip.

Play 17 steps. A perfect opponent would win, so look for the moment the computer leaves you a multiple of 4 that is not in the table of lost positions.
